Surface properties of polyamidines
F. Bo¨hme \*, C. Klinger, C. Bellmann
Institute of Polymer Research Dresden, Hohe Str. 6, D-01069 Dresden, Germany
Received 13 September 1999; accepted 27 April 2000
Abstract

Aromatic and aliphatic polyamidines of the common structure $- ( \mathbf { R } _ { 1 } - \mathbf { N } = \mathbf { C } ( \mathbf { R } _ { 2 } ) - \mathbf { N } \mathbf { H } ) _ { n } -$were investigated by electrokinetic measurements in dependence on the pH value. It could be evidenced, that all polyamidine surfaces show Brønsted basic behaviour. $\mathsf { p } K _ { \mathrm { A } }$values of the surfaces between 7 and 11 were calculated. Particularly, the aliphatic polyamidines $( { \bf R } _ { 1 } , { \bf R } _ { 2 } = \mathrm { a l k y l } )$has proven to be strongly basic. The surface properties correlate well with the basic behaviour of the polyamidines in solution. Furthermore, the surface charge density of the different solid substances was determined. It was found that in the case of aromatic polyamidines $( \mathbf { R } _ { 1 } = \mathrm { a r y l } )$the charge density is dependent on specific interactions of the amidine groups in the solid phase. Especially, in polyformamidines mutual shielding of the amidine groups by hydrogen bonds resulted in reduced charge densities on the surface. © 2001 Elsevier Science B.V. All rights reserved.
Keywords: Polyamidines; Surface properties; Electrokinetic investigation; Zeta potential; Acid–base properties
1. Introduction

Interactions on polymer surfaces and interfaces play an important role in many applications. They influence mechanical and adhesive properties of composite materials, where a polymer is at least one part of the composite. One possibility to increase these interactions is the introduction of polar groups into the main chain. Typical examples are polyamides and polyurethanes, the linking groups of which exhibit strong hydrogen bondings [1].

Low molecular amidines are well known structures which are able to undergo numerous interactions [2]. Particularly, their very pronounced basic behaviour has to be emphasized. It was our intention to transfer these properties to polymer materials. Polyamidines with both nitrogen atoms in the main chain $( \mathbf { R } _ { 1 } - \mathbf { N } = \mathbf { C } ( \mathbf { R } _ { 2 } ) – \mathbf { N H } ) _ { n }$are available by the reaction of diamines with orthoesters as described first by Mathias and Overberger [3,4]. This procedure was used for the preparation of various aliphatic and aromatic polyamidines [5–7]. Other synthetic pathways has also been described in the literature [8–10].

As shown earlier, the properties and interactions of aromatic polyamidines are strongly determined by the residue R at the C-Atom of the amidine group [7]. It is assumed that the basic behaviour of polyamidines also depends on the residue R and on the nature of the monomer units used. Different electron donating effects of the substituents may alter $\mathsf { p } K _ { \mathrm { A } }$values of amidines significantly [11]. The aim of the present article is to compare the acid–base properties of polyamidines 1 on the surface and in solution. For this electrokinetic investigations and acid– base titration in solution were carried out.

Electrokinetic phenomena can be observed on solid surfaces which are in contact with a streaming polar liquid. According to Lyklema [12] dissociation of surface groups, preferential adsorption of cations or anions, adsorption of polyelectrolytes and surfactants, isomorphic substitution of cations and anions, and accumulation or depletion of electrons may result in a potential gradient at the interface of such systems.

Generally, the charge distribution at the interface can be described by the model of Gouy and Chapman which was completed by Stern and Grahame [13,14]. This model considers an electric double layer consisting of an immobile layer directly on the solid surface and a diffuse layer. Between these two layers a shear or slipping plane is assumed. Externally applied electrical or mechanical forces result in a relative motion between the immobile and the diffuse layer. The measurable potential at this point is called electrokinetic or zeta () potential. From the dependency of the zeta potential on pH value, surface active agents, etc. valuable information about the nature of the solid surfaces can be drawn.
2. Experimental
. . Materials
1,10-Decanediamine, triethylorthoacetate, triethylorthobenzoate were purchased from Fluka and used without further purification.
. . Polycondensation

The synthesis of the aromatic polyamidines 1a– 1e was described earlier [7]. The aliphatic polyamidines 1f and 1g were synthesized as follows: A mixture of 47.5 mmol of 1,10-decanediamine, 50 mmol of triethylorthobenzoate or triethylorthoacetate, respectively, and 40 mmol of acetic acid was heated under nitrogen from 80 to $1 2 0 \mathrm { { } ^ { \circ } C }$with stirring and continuous removing of the resulting alcohol by distillation. The temperature was kept for 105 min at $1 2 0 \mathrm { { } ^ { \circ } C }$. Then the pressure was reduced to 5 mbar and the temperature was raised stepwise to $1 8 0 \mathrm { { } ^ { \circ } C }$within 45 min. After another 135 min the reaction was completed. A similar procedure was used for 1h. Since solidification occurred during the synthesis the temperature was finally raised to $2 2 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$
The structure of the polymers 1a–1g was confirmed by NMR and titration of the amidine groups. Polyamidine 1h was insoluble and infusible.
. . Zeta potential measurements

Zeta potential measurements were carried out on pulverized samples suspended in electrolytic solutions (0.01 wt.%) using a Zeta Sizer 3 (Malvern Instruments, Malvern, Worcestershire, UK). The velocity of the particles in an electric field of 100 V was measured by Laser Doppler Anemometry using a He/Ne laser beam. In order to keep other influences such as surface conductivity and flow induced electrophoretic retardation negligible, all measurements were performed in KCl solutions with a relatively high salt concentration of 0.001 mol l<sup>−1</sup>. These conditions ensure constant ion strength of the bulk solution during the pH dependent measurements and made it possible to use Eq. (1) for semiquantitative interpretation of electrokinetic results.

The suspensions were treated with an ultrasonic horn, to facilitate the complete dispersion of the particles. To determine the zeta potential as a function of pH, 0.1 m HCl and 0.1 m KOH were used to adjust pH values.

Before comparative measurements were started, the influences of molecular weight, period of exposure in water and traces of catalyst on the level of zeta potential (plateau phase) and the position of the isoelectric point (pH-value were zeta potential equals zero) were checked. The curves remained almost unchanged by these influences. Only the type of catalyst effected the level of the positive zeta potentials slightly. However, the deviations caused by the catalyst were significantly smaller than the structural influences.
. . Titration

The amidine group content of the polymers was determined by potentiometric titration using a Mettler DL 70 titrator (electrode Mettler DG 113-SC). A total of 100 mg of polyamidine were dissolved in 40 ml ethanol (1f–1g) or DMSO (1a–1e) and titrated with 1 N aqueous HCl standard solution. From the titration curves, the $\mathsf { p } K _ { \mathrm { A } }$values and the amidine contents were calculated. The amidine group contents were slightly lower than expected from the composition (85–95%). This is probably caused by the relatively low molecular weight of the samples or by traces of the acidic catalyst used for the synthesis.
3. Results and discussion

The polymers were synthesized by conversion of diamino compounds with respective orthoesters according to Scheme 1. Compared to the procedure used for the preparation of the aromatic polyamidines 1a–1e [7] the reaction conditions for the preparation of 1f–1h were changed. In order to get high conversions, nearly equimolar amounts of an acidic catalyst had to be added to the reaction mixture. The catalyst (acetic acid) was removed by evaporation at elevated temperatures under reduced pressure. It has to be mentioned that in case of 1f and 1g the acetic acid was strongly bonded to the polymers and could only be removed under drastic conditions. This refers to a pronounced basic behaviour. According to Jacobasch, the shape of the zeta potential-pH-function is influenced by dissociation and adsorption processes on the polymer surface [14–16]. For the polymers under investigation the acid–base equilibrium of the amidine groups shown in Scheme 2 has to be regarded.

Positive zeta potentials are obtained when the amidine groups predominate in their protonated form. After deprotonation the zeta potential becomes negative due to preferred adsorption of hydroxyl ions on the polymer surface at higher pH. The positions of the isoelectric points (IEP) shown in Fig. 1 and Table 2 indicate the change from acidic to basic surface behaviour. In a first approximation the isoelectric points are comparable with $\mathsf { p } K _ { \mathrm { A } }$values of Brønsted acids and bases in solution. Therefore, they can be regarded as a measure for the surface basicity.

Another procedure that regards the surface properties more accurately was established by Bo¨rner and Jacobasch [17]. The model considering dissociation processes relates characteristic parameters of the  (pH) function such as the isoelectric point and the potential of the plateau phase $( \zeta _ { \mathrm { p l a t e a u } } = \zeta ( \mathrm { p H } ) = \mathrm { c o n s t a n t } )$to the $\mathsf { p } K _ { \mathrm { A } }$value:

$$
\mathrm{p} K _ {\mathrm{A}} = \mathrm{pH} _ {\mathrm{b}} + 0. 4 3 4 3 \left[ \frac {F \zeta}{R T} \right.
$$
$\mathrm { p H } _ { \mathrm { b } }$in equation $\operatorname { E q . } \ ( 2 )$is the pH of the bulk solution and F is the Faraday constant.

With a help of a computer program [17,18] $\mathsf { p } K _ { \mathrm { A } }$values of the polyamidine surfaces among other parameters were calculated. The calculation program used is based on a stochastic search procedure which allows to obtain six different parameters like the capacitance between the Helmholz layers $c _ { \mathrm { H P } } .$, the adsorption potentials () of positive and negative ions $( \mathrm { K } ^ { + } , \mathrm { A } ^ { - } , \mathrm { H } ^ { + } , \mathrm { O H } ^ { - } )$and the maximum charge density in the diffuse layer $( \sigma ^ { \mathrm { d i f f } } )$from zeta potential-pH and zeta potential ${ \boldsymbol { \mathbf { \mathit { \mathbf { \mathbf { \Phi } } } } } } ^ { - } \boldsymbol { \mathbf { \mathit { \mathbf { \Phi } } } } ^ { c } ( \mathbf { \mathit { \mathbf { \Phi } } } )$functions $( \boldsymbol { c } _ { 0 } ,$electrolyte concentration). The calculated $\mathsf { p } K _ { \mathrm { A } }$and $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { d i f f } }$values are shown in Table 2. Because of their lower relevance in comparing surface properties of polyamidines the other parameter are not given here.

For comparison purposes $\mathsf { p } K _ { \mathrm { A } }$values of the polyamidines in solution were determined by titration with 0.1 N aqueous HCl in DMSO (1a–1e) and ethanol (1f and 1g), respectively. As an example the titration curve of the polyamidine 1f is shown in Fig. 2. The equivalence point is very pronounced. According to the definition, the $\mathsf { p } K _ { \mathrm { A } }$value corresponds to the pH value at which the protonated and deprotonated amidine groups are

The results clearly show that the surface properties of the polyamidines correlate with their basic behaviour in solution. The isoelectric points and the $\mathsf { p } K _ { \mathrm { A } }$values received from the electrokinetic investigations almost match each other and follow the same tendency as the $\mathsf { p } K _ { \mathrm { A } }$values of the polyamidines in solution. Compared to low molecular amidines [11] the $\mathsf { p } K _ { \mathrm { A } }$values of the respective polyamidines in solution are slightly lower. This can be explained by the coiled structure of the polymer.

From The results one can conclude that the substituents on the amidine group have a significant influence on the basic behaviour. The aromatic polyamidines 1a–1e possess isoelectric points at relatively low pH values in the range 7.0–8.0 and $\mathsf { p } K _ { \mathrm { A } }$values on the surface between 7.2 and 8.1. Within this series the values dependent on the electron donating effect of the residue ${ \bf R } _ { 2 }$at the amidine group. The highest values were found for the polyacylamidines 1b–1d since the alkyl residues at the amidine group rather act as electron donor than the proton in 1a or the phenyl group in 1e. From the measurements we can conclude that the surfaces of the aromatic polyamidines possess medium basicity.

elements.text: Distinctly more pronounced basicity were shown by polyamidines substituted with aliphatic groups on both nitrogens. The isoelectric point of 1h was found at pH 11.2 and that one of 1g was beyond the measuring range of our equipment. This behaviour clearly shows that the additional electron donating effect of the aliphatic units on both sides of the amidine group increase the basicity of polyamidines significantly. Taking into account that completely aliphatic low molecular amidines have $\mathsf { p } K _ { \mathrm { A } }$values of approximately 12.5 [11] one can expect similar values for respective polymers. This is confirmed by the $\mathsf { p } K _ { \mathrm { A } }$value (11.0) of 1g in solution. Polyamidine 1f could not be investigated by electrokinetic measurements since it was liquid at room temperature, but its $\mathsf { p } K _ { \mathrm { A } }$in solution reveals medium basicity.

Generally, the number of functional groups or charged centres $( N _ { \mathrm { a } } )$on the surface can be concluded from the $\zeta _ { \mathrm { p l a t e a u } } { \mathrm { - v a l u e } }$. Similar conclusions can be drawn from the charge density in the diffuse layer $( \sigma ^ { \mathrm { d i f f } } )$which can be obtained by the Bo¨rner-Jacobasch model mentioned above. The calculated $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { d i f f } }$values of the polyamidines 1a–1h are shown in Table 2.

The distinctly lower $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { d i f f } }$and $\zeta _ { \mathrm { p l a t e a u } }$-values of the polyformamidine 1a can be explained by its solid phase structure. It was shown earlier [19,20] that the amidine groups in 1a adopt $E \mathrm { - }$syn configuration preferably, resulting in formation of cyclic dimers (see Scheme 3). These cyclic dimers promote fast proton exchange in solution and in the solid phase as evidenced by NMR spectroscopy. Due to the strong interactions polyformamidine 1a is highly crystalline. In contrast with this, E-anti configuration is predominant in polyamidines 1b–1e. In this configuration formation of hydrogen bonds and prototropic tautomerism is retarded. These polymers are amorphous. The interactions lead to a mutual shielding of the amidine groups in 1a resulting in reduction of functional groups on the surface.

Although a direct comparison with the aliphatic polyamidines is problematic due to the completely different structure it seems that the relatively low $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { d i f f } }$value of 1h is also caused by interactions in the bulk. The infusibility of this sample points to a high degree of crystallinity.
4. Conclusions

By analogy with low molecular amidines, polyamidines were expected to show basic behaviour. Both, the investigations of the polymer surface properties by electrokinetic measurements and the investigations of the polymers in solution evidenced basic behaviour of all polyamidines. From the position of the isoelectric points and the $\mathsf { p } K _ { \mathrm { A } }$values calculated with the model of Bo¨rner and Jacobasch as well as the $\mathsf { p } K _ { \mathrm { A } }$values obtained for polymer solutions, the influence of the substituents $\mathsf { R } _ { 1 }$and ${ \bf R } _ { 2 }$on the basic bahaviour of polyamidines can be estimated. From our results one can conclude that electron donating residues at the amidine groups such as alkyl groups increase the basic behaviour of the polyamidines. This influence is particularly pronounced for the $\mathsf { R } _ { 1 }$substituent. According to these findings the following sequence of the basicities can be drawn: aromatic polyformamidines=aromatic polybenzamidinesaromatic polyacylamidinesaliphatic polybenzamidinesaliphatic polyacylamidines.
The same sequence was found for low molecular amidines [11].

Apart from the effect of the substituents, the surface properties were influenced by intramolecular interactions. The maximum charge density on the surface was found to be significantly lower for the polymers 1a and 1g. These polymers have strong hydrogen bonds in the bulk resulting in a high crystallinity. Due to these interactions the functional groups are mutually shielded so that they are not active on the surface.
